nameStory: The 'roundleaf' part of this plant's name comes from its notably round-shaped leaves, which help distinguish it from its many serviceberry cousins. 'Shadbush' is a traditional name because these shrubs bloom when shad fish swim upstream to spawn in spring rivers. It's also called 'red-twigged shadbush' for its distinctive reddish young branches that catch the eye even in winter.
description: Roundleaf shadbush is a medium-sized shrub that grows up to about 10 feet tall, making it one of the smaller members of the serviceberry family. This native New England plant produces clusters of white flowers in spring, followed by sweet, edible berries that start red and ripen to deep purple-blue by summer. Like all serviceberries, it's part of the rose family, and you can see the family resemblance in its five-petaled flowers. The shrub has a neat, rounded growth habit that makes it attractive in both wild and garden settings.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: The leaves are notably round to oval-shaped with fine teeth along the edges, feeling smooth to slightly fuzzy when young. They're typically broader than other serviceberries, with a rounded base and tip that gives them an almost circular appearance.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: White flowers appear in drooping clusters of 4-10 blooms in late spring, each with five narrow petals that feel papery to the touch. The flowers have a light, sweet fragrance and numerous stamens that give them a slightly fuzzy appearance in the center.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: The berries start bright red in early summer and ripen to dark purple-blue, feeling firm and smooth with a sweet, slightly almond-like flavor. These aren't true berries but pomes (like tiny apples) with small seeds inside that crunch when you bite them.

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Young twigs are distinctively reddish to purplish-brown, smooth to the touch, which gives this species its alternate name 'red-twigged shadbush.' Older bark becomes gray and develops shallow furrows.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms a dense, multi-stemmed shrub typically 6-10 feet tall with an upright but rounded shape. The branches often arch slightly outward, creating an attractive vase-like silhouette.

habitat: Roundleaf shadbush thrives in rocky or sandy soils in open woodlands, forest edges, and clearings throughout New England's mountains and hills. You'll often find it growing alongside other understory shrubs like elderberry and dogwood, particularly in areas with good drainage and partial sunlight. It's especially common in the northern parts of New England where cooler conditions suit its preferences.

seasonality.spring: White flower clusters bloom in late April to May, creating showy displays just as the leaves are emerging. The flowers appear before the shrub is fully leafed out, making identification easier.
seasonality.summer: Berries ripen from red to dark purple-blue in July and August, while the green foliage provides a lush backdrop. This is prime time for both fruit identification and harvesting.
seasonality.fall: Leaves turn brilliant shades of orange, red, and yellow, making it one of the more spectacular fall shrubs. The colorful foliage makes it easy to spot even from a distance.
seasonality.winter: The reddish-brown twigs become the main identifying feature, along with the multi-stemmed growth pattern and small, pointed buds. Old fruit clusters may persist into early winter.

funFact: The berries of roundleaf shadbush were so important to Indigenous peoples that some tribes planned their seasonal movements around the fruiting time, and early European settlers learned to make pies and jams from them that were said to taste better than blueberries!
confusionNotes: With eight different serviceberry species in New England, telling them apart can be tricky! Focus on the leaf shape - roundleaf shadbush has the most circular leaves of the bunch, while most others have more oval or elongated leaves. The reddish young twigs are also a dead giveaway - remember 'red twigs, round leaves' as your memory trick.
contextualKnowledge: The term 'serviceberry' itself comes from 'sarvisberry,' an old Appalachian pronunciation, while 'Juneberry' (another common name for the genus) refers to when most species fruit. However, roundleaf shadbush often fruits in July-August, so don't let the 'June' name throw you off timing-wise.
compareHints: Among New England's serviceberries, roundleaf shadbush stands out with its notably circular leaves and red-tinted twigs - most others have more elongated, oval leaves and gray-brown branches. It's also typically shorter and more shrub-like than common serviceberry, which can become tree-sized, and bushier than the low-growing running serviceberry.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's serviceberry species, common serviceberry stands out for its fuzzy young leaves - smooth shadbush has (as the name suggests) smooth leaf undersides, while Canadian serviceberry has more elongated flower clusters.
Unlike its taller cousins like Common Serviceberry or Smooth Shadbush that can reach 15-25 feet, Nantucket Shadbush stays under 5 feet and spreads horizontally rather than growing upward.
Among New England's serviceberries, smooth shadbush stands out for its completely hairless leaves and twigs - most other species have at least some fuzziness, especially when young.
Bartram shadbush is smaller and more mountain-loving than common serviceberry, which grows into a proper tree.
Canadian serviceberry differs from its relatives by preferring wet habitats and forming colonies through underground runners, while common serviceberry grows as single trees in drier upland areas.

Running Serviceberry is easily distinguished from other New England serviceberries by its low, colony-forming growth habit - no other serviceberry in the region spreads aggressively through underground runners.
Intermediate serviceberry sits right between its parent species in terms of leaf fuzziness and fall color intensity.
Low serviceberry differs from its taller relatives like common serviceberry and smooth shadbush by its shrubby, colony-forming growth habit rather than single-trunk tree form.
